title: My Six-Year-Old Told Me to Say No to AI
author: Sam Illingworth
summary: Sam Illingworth examines the decisions by New York City and Los Angeles Unified to switch off student-facing generative AI for well over a million children, and asks whether prohibition works in education. He first gives the strongest case for the bans: unassessed vendors create real legal exposure, research such as a PNAS field experiment shows students who lean on GPT-4 perform worse once it is removed, and a blanket ban is the only intervention that reaches every child equally. He then tests prohibition against two precedents, abstinence-only sex education and school phone bans, both of which showed little or no measurable benefit. His central move is to argue that design, not access, changes outcomes: the same PNAS study found a guardrailed GPT Tutor largely removed the crutch effect, and Character.AI's removal of open-ended chat for minors reached children everywhere. A school ban, he contends, removes supervised access while leaving unsupervised use at home, falling hardest on students without informed parents. He supports prohibiting companion chatbots for children and offers five alternatives, from asking children what they think to asking what design change would address the harm.
points: New York City and Los Angeles have switched off student-facing generative AI for well over a million children, with legal data-protection risk a central and often overlooked reason.
A PNAS study found students who practised with GPT-4 did 17% worse once it was removed, but a guardrailed GPT Tutor version largely eliminated that crutch effect.
Illingworth compares AI bans to abstinence-only education and school phone bans, both of which showed little measurable effect in rigorous studies.
Bans remove supervised, teacher-visible use while leaving home use untouched, which widens gaps for students without informed parents.
He endorses one restriction, keeping companion chatbots from children, and argues that changing how a product behaves beats restricting access at the school gate.
quotes: There is a genuine legal issue. A district cannot lawfully hand a child’s data to a vendor it has not assessed, and every tool needs an assessment, a contract, an age check and a retention policy.
They had used AI as a crutch, and when the crutch went the walking had not been learned.
The same researchers ran a version called GPT Tutor: the identical model, with guardrails built into how it answered. The crutch effect largely disappeared. What fixed it was how the thing was built.
A school ban removes the supervised, teacher-visible version of a tool. It does not remove the tool.
It is the same finding as GPT Tutor. Change how the thing behaves and the harm moves. Remove access at the school gate and the harm walks home.
Not how to prompt. When is this system guessing, who profits from me believing it, and what is it doing to my own thinking while I use it.
Prohibition can be implemented in a fortnight and educational change can take a decade (or longer!), so of course one of them keeps arriving first.
